source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: ToT frames problem solving as search over a tree of thoughts. A design has four parts: how to split the work into thought steps, how to generate thoughts, how to evaluate states, and which search algorithm to run. It draws on Newell, Shaw and Simon and on System 1 / System 2 thinking.
numbers: Four design questions. Search is BFS (keep the b best states per step) or DFS (go deep, prune below a value threshold, backtrack). IO, CoT, CoT-SC and self-refine are called special cases of ToT (trees of limited depth and breadth).
quote: IO, CoT, CoT-SC, and self-refinement can be seen as special cases of ToT
limits: Only BFS and DFS tested. A* and MCTS left to future work. Thought size is chosen by hand per task.
agent_relevance: Our S6 idea tree needs these four choices fixed in code: thought unit, generator, evaluator, search rule.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Game of 24 (GPT-4): ToT beat every sampling baseline by a wide margin. Even breadth 1 gave 45%.
numbers: 100 hard games (4nums indices 901-1000). IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC (k=100) 9.0%, IO+refine (k=10, uses ground-truth feedback) 27%, IO best of 100 33%, CoT best of 100 49%, ToT b=1 45%, ToT b=5 74%. Proposal prompt gives next equations; value prompt says sure/maybe/impossible, sampled 3 times.
limits: One task, 100 games, one run per setting, GPT-4, May 2023. Hardest-ranked slice of games. Later work reports lower ToT numbers (see a15).
agent_relevance: A code-checkable sure/impossible pruner on a small step space produced the gain. Fits G5 (code selects) when the check can be coded.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Error analysis on Game of 24: about 60% of CoT samples were already dead after the first step (the first three words, e.g. '4 + 9'). Left-to-right decoding commits too early.
numbers: About 60% of CoT samples failed at step 1. ToT b=5 kept the failure share lower at every step (Fig 3b, read from a figure).
limits: Per-step ToT numbers are not tabulated.
agent_relevance: Supports branching at the first step of a plan, where one early choice kills most runs.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Creative Writing: ToT used sample-then-vote at two steps (plan, then passage), breadth 1. Quality rose, but the judge was GPT-4 itself.
numbers: 100 inputs. GPT-4 coherence score (1-10, mean of 5, sd about 0.56): IO 6.19, CoT 6.93, ToT 7.56. Human blind pairs (a subset of the authors): ToT better in 41, CoT better in 21, similar in 38. Iterative refine: IO 6.19 to 7.67, ToT 7.56 to 7.91.
limits: No ground truth. Judge is an LLM. Human raters were authors. Refine on IO came close to ToT at lower cost.
agent_relevance: Voting over plans is cheap, but the metric is a model judge. Our G5 says a judge must be blind and length-normalised.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Mini Crosswords (5x5): DFS with a state evaluator that prunes when any remaining clue looks impossible. Both backtracking and pruning matter in the ablations.
numbers: 20 test games. Word-level success: IO 14%, CoT 15.6%, ToT 60%. Letters: 38.7 / 40.6 / 78. Games solved: 0 / 1 / 4 of 20. Oracle best state: 82.4% letters, 67.5% words, 7/20 games. No prune: 65.4 letters, 41.5 words, 1 game. No backtrack: 54.6 letters, 20 words, 1 game. DFS capped at 100 steps.
limits: 20 games only. The evaluator pruned solved boards when GPT-4 did not know a rare word (e.g. 'agend'). Unpruned search found 4/20 solutions, 3 that pruned search missed.
agent_relevance: A false 'impossible' verdict prunes the right branch. Keep pruning revisable, or log pruned nodes.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: Weaker model and split roles: on Game of 24 the bottleneck is thought generation, not evaluation.
numbers: GPT-3.5 ToT 19% vs GPT-4 ToT 74% (proposal prompt changed from 1-shot to 3-shot for GPT-3.5). GPT-4 generate + GPT-3.5 evaluate 64%. GPT-3.5 generate + GPT-4 evaluate 31%. Creative Writing: GPT-3.5 IO 4.47, CoT 5.16, ToT 6.62.
limits: One task per claim. Appendix tables.
agent_relevance: A cheap model may judge nodes while a stronger one proposes them. Test on our own tasks.

source: Yao et al. (2023) Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
finding: ToT costs far more than CoT and gains little on easy tasks.
numbers: Game of 24: ToT 5.5k completion + 1.4k prompt tokens, $0.74 per case, 74%; CoT best of 100 6.7k + 2.2k tokens, $0.47, 49%; IO best of 100 $0.13, 33%. Creative Writing: ToT about 5x the cost of CoT. Authors say 5-100x more generated tokens than CoT. Zero-shot ToT on GSM8K 90 vs CoT 86; StrategyQA 83 vs 82 (100 questions each).
limits: Some cost-table rows are misaligned in the PDF text. GSM8K/StrategyQA gains are small and on 100 items.
agent_relevance: Search should be tied to a signal (G1): use it where plain sampling fails, not on easy items.

source: Long (2023) Large Language Model Guided Tree-of-Thought
finding: A concurrent, separate ToT: an LLM prompter agent, a rule-based checker, a memory module and a ToT controller that backtracks. Tested on small Sudoku.
numbers: 10 puzzles each at 3x3, 4x4, 5x5. Zero/one/few-shot CoT solvers fall to about 0.5 on larger boards. ToT solves 10/10 at 3x3, 9/10 at 4x4 (1 failure within 100 rounds), 8/10 at 5x5. Paper states ToT is 80% higher than one/few-shot at 4x4 and 60% higher at 5x5.
limits: Tiny benchmark (10 puzzles per size). Controller is rule-based and does not know whether a partial board can be completed. A learned (REINFORCE) controller is proposed, not tested.
agent_relevance: Same shape as our design: model proposes, code checks and backtracks. A code checker is the strongest evaluator when one exists.

source: Hao et al. (2023) Reasoning with Language Model is Planning with World Model (RAP)
finding: RAP uses the LLM as both agent and world model and runs MCTS over reasoning steps. The reward mixes action likelihood, self-evaluation and state confidence.
numbers: Blocksworld, LLaMA-33B, 2/4/6-step success: RAP(10) 1.00 / 0.86 / 0.26, RAP(20) 1.00 / 0.88 / 0.42, vs CoT with GPT-4 0.50 / 0.63 / 0.40. Mean RAP 64%; paper claims 33% relative gain over GPT-4 CoT. GSM8K: CoT 29.4, CoT+SC(10) 46.8, RAP(1) 48.6, RAP(10) 51.6. PrOntoQA: CoT 87.8 answer / 64.8 proof, RAP 94.2 / 78.8.
limits: LLaMA-33B vs GPT-4 is a cross-model comparison. Reward terms are tuned per task (action likelihood is key for planning, little help for math). Self-evaluation reward is weakly reliable (see a17).
agent_relevance: An explicit state after each action prevented illegal plans. Our schema keeps state in code, a stricter version.

source: Hao et al. (2023) RAP
finding: On the full Blocksworld (602 cases, Llama-2 70B) RAP helps but still decays with plan length.
numbers: Easy setting mean: CoT 0.08, RAP(10) 0.65. Hard setting: CoT 0.05, RAP(10) 0.51. Easy by length for RAP: 2-step 1.00, 4-step 0.99, 6-step 0.75, 8-step 0.61, 10-step 0.32. CoT is near 0 beyond 6 steps.
limits: In the Easy setting demonstrations match the test step count, which leaks information. 10-case demonstration pools.
agent_relevance: Success falls with depth even with search. Cap tree depth or decompose the task.

source: Xie et al. (2023) Self-Evaluation Guided Beam Search for Reasoning
finding: Stochastic beam search where each step is scored by the model's likelihood times a self-evaluation (is this step correct?). Better calibrated than likelihood alone.
numbers: Codex. GSM8K PAL single chain 72.0 to 80.2 (27.7k tokens vs 0.3k); multi-chain 80.4 (PAL-SC, 7.4k tokens) to 85.5 (550k tokens). AQuA 64.2 vs 58.6 (PoT-SC). StrategyQA 73.2 to 77.2 (11.6k vs 0.06k tokens). CommonsenseQA 77.9 to 78.6; Sports 98.5 vs 98.4. Setting the mix weight to 1 or 0 drops GSM8K from 80.2 to 74.5 or 77.1.
limits: Very high cost at full settings. Equal-cost test (Llama-2 13B): 46.1% at 12.6k tokens vs self-consistency 41.8% at 13.9k. Needs token logits, so not run on ChatGPT or GPT-4. No gain where the baseline is near ceiling (Sports; Object Counting 96.7).
agent_relevance: Self-evaluation helps as a tie-breaker between near-equal steps. Gains grow with chain length (their Table 4). Use for long chains only.

source: Xie et al. (2023) Self-Evaluation Guided Beam Search for Reasoning
finding: Backbone comparison: a stronger model with no search can beat a weaker model with search.
numbers: GSM8K: CoT Codex 65.6, CoT ChatGPT 80.8, CoT GPT-4 92.0, PAL ChatGPT 78.7, search+PAL Codex 80.2. StrategyQA: CoT ChatGPT 65.9, search+CoT Codex 77.2.
limits: ChatGPT numbers dated 20 March 2023. Prompting forms differ.
agent_relevance: Spend on a stronger base model before spending on search width.

source: Besta et al. (2023) Graph of Thoughts: Solving Elaborate Problems with Large Language Models
finding: GoT lets thoughts be vertices in an arbitrary graph, with Generate, Aggregate (merge several thoughts) and Refine loops. It adds a latency-volume trade-off measure.
numbers: Volume of a thought = number of earlier thoughts that can reach it. CoT latency N, volume N. CoT-SC latency N/k, volume N/k. ToT latency log_k N, volume O(log_k N). GoT latency log_k N and volume N. Tasks: sorting, set intersection, keyword counting, document merging, all with ChatGPT-3.5.
limits: Volume and latency are idealised counts, not wall-clock. Authors tried Llama-2: worse and too slow.
agent_relevance: Merging partial solutions (aggregate) is a graph move a tree cannot make. Maps to a code-run merge step in S6.

source: Besta et al. (2023) Graph of Thoughts
finding: GoT beats ToT, CoT and IO on decomposable tasks, and the margin grows with problem size. It is also cheaper than ToT.
numbers: Sorting: median error 61% lower than ToT at P=64 and 69% lower at P=128 (abstract: 62% over ToT with over 31% lower cost). Versus CoT and IO at P=64: 65% and 83% lower median error. At P=32 GoT only slightly beat ToT. GoT cost always below ToT, comparable to ToT2.
limits: ChatGPT-3.5 only. Tasks chosen because they split into subtasks by hand (merge-sort style). The graph of operations is written by hand per task. Scores are code-computed, not LLM-judged.
agent_relevance: The gain came from splitting a large job into small ones the model gets right, then merging. Evidence for decomposition more than for search.

source: Sel et al. (2023) Algorithm of Thoughts: Enhancing Exploration of Ideas in Large Language Models
finding: AoT puts whole search traces (with dead ends and backtracks) in one prompt so the model explores in a single query. Its own ToT numbers are below the original paper's.
numbers: Game of 24: IO 7.3%, CoT 4.0%, CoT-SC 9.0% (100 queries), ToT(b=5) 69% with 109.1 queries and 13,900 prompt / 5,500 completion tokens, AoT 71% with 1 query and 5,450 / 998.4 tokens. AoT with manual resolution of failures 78%. Mini crosswords word success: IO 14%, CoT-SC 15.6%, ToT 46.5% (over 200 queries, 96,700 prompt tokens), AoT 52% (2 queries).
limits: Text is unclear whether ToT was rerun or copied. ToT 69% (Game 24) and 46.5% (crosswords) are lower than ToT's own 74% and 60%. 20 crossword games. AoT crossword errors: erroneous word placement 52.6%, incorrect pattern extraction 26.3%, no preselections 15.8%, expression misstep 5.3%.
agent_relevance: One call with a worked search trace roughly matches multi-call tree search at about 1/100 of the queries. A cheap route for S6 if the trace format holds.

source: Sel et al. (2023) Algorithm of Thoughts
finding: AoT adds that fine-tuning on search traces still helps, and ToT's gain on common QA is small.
numbers: Fine-tuning on Game of 24 with 900 examples compared AoT vs CoT traces (their Table 5). Zero-shot GSM8K / StrategyQA: CoT 86% / 82%, ToT 90% / 83% (taken from the ToT paper). AoT gives a slight boost on GPT-4.
limits: Per-task prompt design. Authors state AoT still needs more tokens than CoT; GPT-4 for main tests.
agent_relevance: Search traces in context transfer to knowledge-light math puzzles, less to knowledge tasks.

source: Feng et al. (2023/2024) AlphaZero-Like Tree-Search can Guide Large Language Model Decoding and Training (TS-LLM)
finding: With a learned value function, tree search beats prompt-based self-evaluation by a wide margin. This directly tests the ToT/RAP assumption that the LLM can value its own states.
numbers: BFS Path@1, LLaMA-SFT policy: Game24 9.2 with LLaMA prompted value, 21.0 with GPT-3.5 prompted value (ToT), 64.8 with learned LLaMA-V. GSM8K 37.4 / 45.8 / 52.5. With GPT-3.5 policy: Game24 15.5 vs 19.1; GSM8K 72.7 vs 74.0. Greedy CoT: GSM8K 41.4, Game24 12.7, PrOntoQA 48.8.
limits: Learned value needs training data from rollouts. The PDF table layout is garbled; attribution of rows to tasks checked against the greedy row and the 64.8 figure. Authors cite Huang 2023 and Stechly 2023 for weak prompted self-evaluation.
agent_relevance: Strong support for G2/G5: a prompted LLM judge is a weak state value. Prefer code checks or trained scorers.

source: Feng et al. (2023/2024) TS-LLM
finding: Under equal token budgets the search advantage shrinks on shallow tasks. Search wins most where the plan is deep.
numbers: Path@1: GSM8K CoT-greedy 41.4, BFS-V 52.5, MCTS-alpha 51.9; Game24 12.7, 64.8, 63.3; PrOntoQA 48.8, 94.4, 99.4. Equal-token: CoT-SC with learned reward model 52.3 on GSM8K (BFS-V 52.5), 50.6 on Game24 vs search 69-71, PrOntoQA 83.2 vs 96-99.6. Tree depth up to 64 (RLHF and chess endgame).
limits: Authors say CoT-SC beats tree search on GSM8K at equal tokens mainly because it explores more distinct sentences. Aggregation helps tree search less on small problems.
agent_relevance: On short-horizon math, sample-and-rerank is competitive. Reserve search for deep or branchy problems.

source: Gandhi et al. (2024) Stream of Search (SoS): Learning to Search in Language
finding: Training a small LM on search traces that include mistakes and backtracking beats training on optimal paths only. Search is written as one flat string, no controller.
numbers: Countdown. SoS-pretrained model 51.27% on held-out inputs vs 25.73% for the optimal-path model. Only 57.1% (285,501) of training trajectories reach the goal. After APA / STaR finetuning the model solves about 36% of previously unsolved problems and about 4% of difficult ones that no heuristic solver solved.
limits: Trained from scratch on a toy game. No prompt-only claim. 95% binomial intervals reported.
agent_relevance: Showing the model its own dead ends helps. In a scaffold with no training the nearest move is feeding back real failed attempts (G2).

source: Lehnert et al. (2024) Beyond A*: Better Planning with Transformers via Search Dynamics Bootstrapping (Searchformer)
finding: A transformer trained to emit A* execution traces, then fine-tuned to shorten them, plans better than one trained on plans alone.
numbers: Searchformer solves unseen Sokoban puzzles optimally 93.7% of the time using up to 26.8% fewer search steps than the A* used for training. Beats solution-only baselines with 5-10x smaller models and 10x smaller training data.
limits: Synthetic mazes and Sokoban; encoder-decoder trained from scratch, not an off-the-shelf LLM.
agent_relevance: Tracing the search in text helps more than the final answer alone, but only when trained on it.

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Compares best-of-N, beam search and lookahead search against a process reward model (PRM) on MATH with PaLM 2-S*. Search helps at small budgets and on mid-hard items, and hurts on easy ones.
numbers: Beam search clearly beats best-of-N at small budgets, but at higher budgets (up to 256 generations) it often falls below best-of-N. Lookahead search (k=3 or 1 steps; cost counted as N x (k+1)) usually underperforms at equal budget. By difficulty: levels 1-2 beam search gets worse as budget grows; levels 3-4 beam search beats best-of-N; level 5 no method makes progress. Compute-optimal choice by difficulty matches best-of-N with about 4x less compute.
limits: Math only, one PRM, one model family. Authors blame exploiting the PRM (repetitive low-information steps, solutions of only 1-2 steps). Model-estimated difficulty bins predicted efficacy better than hand labels.
agent_relevance: Search can over-optimise a weak scorer. Match search depth to difficulty and to scorer reliability (links G1, G5).

source: Wu et al. (2024/2025) Inference Scaling Laws: An Empirical Analysis of Compute-Optimal Inference for Problem-Solving with Language Models
finding: Cost-performance study of greedy, majority vote, best-of-n, weighted vote, MCTS and a new tree search, REBASE. MCTS pairs poorly with weighted voting.
numbers: MCTS often leaves many unfinished solutions, so fewer votes. REBASE (no rollouts; a node-quality reward sets how much each node expands) beats sampling and MCTS across settings. Llemma-7B + REBASE beats Llemma-34B under all strategies tested on MATH, and matches Llemma-34B accuracy with about 2x fewer FLOPs on MATH500 and GSM8K. Sampling and REBASE saturate early on GSM8K, later on MATH.
limits: Math with Llemma and Mistral and a reward model; saturation bounded by policy output probabilities (their proof).
agent_relevance: A cheap tree search that keeps many finished branches beat classic MCTS on cost. Rollout-free expansion is easier to code in our loop.

source: Koh et al. (2024/2026) Tree Search for Language Model Agents
finding: Best-first tree search inside a real web environment (VisualWebArena, WebArena) with an LM value function. Gains grow with depth and breadth, but absolute scores stay low.
numbers: VWA full 910 tasks: GPT-4o + SoM 18.9% to 26.4% (+39.7% relative). Llama-3-70B + captions 7.6% to 16.7% (+119.7%). WebArena 812 tasks: GPT-4o 15.0% to 19.2% (+28.0%); Llama-3-70B 7.6% to 10.1% (+32.3%). On 200 VWA tasks, budget c=20: baseline about 24.5%; shallow settings 26.0% (+6%); then 32.0% (+31%), 31.5% (+29%), 35.0% (+43%), 35.5% (+45%); best setting 37.0% (+51%).
limits: Backtracking needs an environment reset (replay the action sequence). Irreversible actions must be blocked from expansion. Extra API cost; value function imperfect. Strong non-search agents score higher on WebArena (AgentOccam 43.1%).
agent_relevance: Search over real actions needs reversibility. In S6 we search over ideas, where a wrong branch is cheap.

source: Newell and Simon (1972) Human Problem Solving, as cited by Yao et al. (2023)
finding: ToT credits Newell, Shaw and Simon for the view that problem solving is search through a combinatorial space guided by heuristics. Second-hand: read only through the ToT paper's text.
numbers: No new numbers. ToT pairs this with dual-process theory, and names A* (Hart et al. 1968) and MCTS as search options it did not test.
limits: Original not read. ToT text only.
agent_relevance: Our S6 follows the classic search view: state, operators, heuristic, stop rule.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning, as used by Yao et al. (2023)
finding: Majority vote over many independent CoT samples. ToT uses it as the main non-search baseline; TS-LLM and Xie et al. test search against it at equal tokens.
numbers: Game of 24: CoT-SC with 100 samples 9.0% (ToT paper). GSM8K at equal tokens, CoT-SC with a learned reward model 52.3 vs BFS-V 52.5 (TS-LLM).
limits: Original paper not opened; numbers come from the opened papers above.
agent_relevance: Sampling plus code-side selection is the baseline any search idea must beat on the same token budget.
